title: How Has the Depiction of Violence Against Women Changed over the Years in Mainstream Films from the United States?

commenti.body:
>However, one of his songs: “Whoop That Trick,” seems to be about striking prostitutes. Let me know if I have misunderstood, as I could very well be wrong. I never understood how this song won best song at the Oscars.

The song isn't about striking prostitutes . Trick is street lingo for a man that pays for sex and is also used to demean a man whether they buy sex or not .

My belief is that with really old movies domestic violence is treated like alcoholism or smoking.. a negative vice that is inconsequential ( I do not agree with this take)

I do think that perhaps what is at  play is the more dramatization of everyday life - - drunkenness is seen as tragic ( days of wine  and roses) James Bond stopped smoking in the nineties, and  domestic abuse kind of fades from a punchline to an antagonizing thing ( the old film Born yesterday is very much a comedy, but the domestic violence inflicted on the main character is played straight)

I think the question "What would a modern audience think?" Is something that has an observable answer ( an IMDb or Letterboxd review or commentary would likely be from a person under 40)  

However I will say this.. often when there's contemporary criticism of something old, there's actually a reviewer from that older era who is thinking along similar lines.  

So what I don't feel is that back in the day everybody thought the same thing, but that audiences were more accepting of certain societal flaws as well as filmmaking styles that are more simplistic ( Matte painting travelogues)
Thank you for the correction. I will take out this example from my post. In retrospect, I should not have included it, as it was the only film of the bunch I had not seen in recent years.

Thank you so much for the thoughtful response. I think your viewpoint on this is very interesting. The idea of domestic violence as simply a negative vice is very unsettling. However, I suppose it is better for me to learn from the mistakes of the past then to judge people when I did not live in that time period.

Violence against women in film is an incredibly tricky subject, and I'm far from an expert.  We know that film has a powerful effect on culture: one of my favourite film critics (tedg) describes both the outlaw motorcycle gang and the italian-american mafia as inseperable from their own view of themselves formed through consuming film - in the first case, I have read, the motorcycle outlaws on film resulted the socially constructed gangs forming afterwards.
So we come to film and it's powerful image and the question of what it means when we see, let's say a woman being strangled on a film poster, brought to lurid heights in the actual film itself.  What does that mean for us, to have these become the tropes through which we build our sense of the world and ourselves?

I don't have any answers.

I'm interested in the way that now we treat violence against women with some amount more sensitivity, we're a bit more careful and restrained in our depictions, outright open violence against women has taken on some elements of (minor) social taboo, and therefore a kind of power. It can be shocking again, and there are directors and filmmakers who are interested in how to use that and place it in a story.

The first example I can think of is the [Italian Spiderman trailer](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UhHhXukovMU&t=42s) which is an incredible parody of 70s tropes.  When the violence happens, recognizing that it's wrong is essential to the joke, that we're watching something from another age and the physics and storytelling and ideas about women are horrible an misogynist.

But we live in the age of memes, and there were memes drawn from this trailer, and when we lift it out of that context and into another the "hero" punching a woman can mean quite a different thing.

I feel similarly unsettled about the opening scene to [The Way of the Gun (2000)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=eQLXYu6plhg).  It's our introduction to the two protagonists, it's very effective in that in a couple of minutes we know everything we need to know about exactly what type of guys this story is about. Ones who think our discomfort about violence against women is stupid and childish.  There's a person on the screen who makes the same assumptions we do about what whether violence against women is acceptable (read: possible in a film wolrd), and look at what happens to her.  In some ways, her position means she acts as a stand-in for us in audience who are watching the film with moral reservations about these sort of things.  And the film reaches out to mess with us.
I think that's incredibly smart filmmaking, that uses our discomfort and our ideas, actually depends on them, in order to make its point.

And then, we are in the age of memes and youtube clips, and we lose the context.  Maybe the original context was "this is a story about the exact kind of guys who would do this horrific thing" and then you see the film and you see how it unfolds for them.  Or maybe the film is leaning in to the exploitation angle and saying "you claim you have scruples but look how obnoxious she way, we know you secretly took pleasure in seeing that, you're not such a moral paragon yourself"

But in 2023, maybe now the context is "here's a youtube clip of violence against women, maybe you'll laugh your ass off for a minute before you move on to something else".  You see it that way, you get a different message from it.  If the artistic meaning and the social point that made this was all in the context, what does it mean when we lift it out of context? What does it mean when maybe most people this year are seeing it this way, instead of part of the complete film, which isn't well-known?  

Does our new media landscape mean we're now trapped and unable to say in film any kind of meaningful layered commentary anymore?  

Am I somehow making it worse, by linking to these clips?  I don't know, I don't have the answers on this.

I would also add that violence against women in films didn't really stop.

Quentin Tarantino didn't seem unfazed by including such in his movies. The only difference is that the application of violence against women had purpose based on the writing he was going for.

True Romance has a scene involving >!one of the main characters, Alabama, fighting for her life against Virgil, an antagonist, and it's such a realistic and violent fight they have.!<

Jackie Brown has a scene involving >!Robert DeNiro's character, Louie, killing Melanie because of her continuing to make fun of him forgetting where they parked.!<

The Hateful Eight has >!Daisy (played by Jennifer Jason Leigh) getting her share of physical beating because of her being a criminal and continuing to be antagonistic despite being in custody to a bounty hunter.!<

Inglourious Basterds, >!we had a couple of ladies in that movie who also had to get their hands dirty and get into real dangerous territory considering the Nazi element within.!<

Even >!Kill Bill Vol 1 & 2 had their share of women engaging in violence, including the protagonist herself, and even against other women at that.!<

I am sure some of his other movies may have other examples missed. But Quentin hasn't been cancelled as of yet. He is still working and making movies, and people still love the heck out of his work.

Thank you for your contribution to this conversation. You make some interesting points. I think the idea that people can use YouTube clips to take violent scenes out of context has merit. It is important to remember the context of violence. I think it is important to grant the filmmakers the right to exercise judgement based on context. However, sometimes the violence becomes dislodged from context in cultural memory.

Edit: From the upvotes and downvotes, this post seems to have had a polarizing effect on people. If anyone could tell me why, I'd appreciate it. I want to continue to improve as a poster. I will take your feedback seriously.

This is a very specific example, but I'd say the idea of the "final girl" in American slasher movies wasn't initially set up as any kind of female empowerment, but rather a way to keep a puerile audience engaged with the promise of nudity all the way through the end of the film (although, ironically given the chaste implications of the post-F13 "you fuck and you die" template, the final girl almost never got naked). 

But as time went on the idea of the "final girl" actually took on a life of it's own, becoming such an ingrained concept in the horror movie that it eventually DID function as a sort of female empowerment. You can especially see that in more modern horror, where obligatory sex/nudity has become almost non-existent... yet the trope remains.

Good take. I'd say for an uncomfortably long time wives were viewed as property as much as human beings, to the point where it wasn't much different than abusing livestock. with the husbands being benevolent benefactors that sometimes had a bad day. But much like whipping a horse, while people would flinch at the idea of it there was also an "understanding" that the horse/wife wouldn't be able to subsist on their own, so there was an ingrained idea that you have to suffer the occasional injustice to make your way in this world. Note that I also don't agree with this, but it's useless to view bygone eras through our own more progressive lens.
I'd argue that in none of Tarantino's films is he glorifying those acts.

Thank you for this insightful response. Your comment that wives were seen as property is a helpful description. Further, the idea that a man might be likened to a benefactor having good days and bad days is a useful analogy. This might explain why in a film a man might suddenly act violently and then later become "normal" again from the modern perspective. For me, as a modern viewer, the change in behavior is incredibly jarring. However, perhaps to some viewers decades ago this might not have been shocking.

You also make a productive comment about the financial ramifications of marriage from a woman's perspective. The link to the economics of marriage explains why a woman would have to endure violence. Otherwise, women might have rebelled against the system more often.

It is deeply sad that women were treated this way. However, your comments have shed light on this issue; thank you for sharing them.

Oh I agree. They aren't meant to be glorified.

It was the writing that led to these moments I outlined above. My point is that Tarantino to this day doesn't shy from violence against women because he also doesn't shy from violence against men. He approaches it soundly enough because of the writing.

“Chinatown” comes to mind.  It seems the slapping of a woman used to be more commonplace in American film and not seen as comparable to a closed-fist punch.  I don’t think any American film has portrayed punching a woman as commonplace;  it’s the slapping that was normalized.  

Don’t forget, though, Cher’s famous slap of Nicolas Cage in the 80’s movie “Moonstruck.”   https://youtu.be/Uz95y3gLNA4?si=V0lBl8dvPDDSKCfD

As late as circa 1980, you had this parody scene from Airplane.  Here again, a slap is likened to a splash of cold water, or to smelling salts.  The idea was that “women who are becoming hysterical need a good slap; the shock will bring them to their senses.”

https://youtu.be/i0GW0Vnr9Yc?si=Oz6ijvPAMkPFtjcb

I won’t include the clip to a comparable scene in “Chinatown,” but it has that same trope of slapping a woman as part of a normal dynamic in a male-female relationship.  

There even is a sense in American culture of it being *disrespectful * for a man to be slapped by another man because it is presumed to be not only the typical way that *women *  strike a blow,  but also the typical way in which men hit women, versus other men (“showing the restraint of a slap”).  The infamous Oscar slap was intended as a form of disrespect in the latter sense.   I knew someone who use to say, “I’ll just bitch slap him” with a similar implication of disrespect — that slaps were traditionally reserved for women and for children (including women slapping children, or slapping men). 

A woman slapping a man’s face as a response to *disrespect*, particularly due to a comment that is sexually inappropriate, was very much of American culture.  

3:58 of “Chasing Amy” (1998) is yet another example.  Here, the man is slapped by a woman for having disrespected her.


And this, from Revenge of the Nerds II, where a slap is an appropriate, or expected, response to a rude come-on.

https://youtu.be/Jj2Lpw9Yeqw?si=lSPH78zpDnkZxafC

America’s attitude towards violence in general — including as regards child-rearing, or as regards what used to be seen as a cautionary, admonishing, slap in the face— would make for just as interesting a study…. And a more all-encompassing one.
